stem: A 42-year-old woman with an 8-year history of plaque psoriasis (treated with topical corticosteroids and intermittent narrowband UVB phototherapy) presents to clinic with new-onset asymmetric oligoarticular arthritis: synovitis of the right wrist, the left knee, and the right second toe with a SAUSAGE-SHAPED DIGIT (DACTYLITIS). Her fingernails show pitting and onycholysis. She has no axial symptoms, no inflammatory bowel symptoms, and no uveitis. Vital signs stable. Labs: rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP NEGATIVE; ESR 38 mm/h; CRP 22 mg/L. Plain radiographs of the affected hands demonstrate erosive changes including the classic 'PENCIL-IN-CUP' deformity at the distal interphalangeal joint. The clinical picture meets the CASPAR criteria for psoriatic arthritis with peripheral and dactylitic features but no axial disease.
question: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Methotrexate (effective for peripheral arthritis and skin disease); for inadequate response or dactylitis/enthesitis-predominant disease — escalate to a TNF inhibitor (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab), an IL-17 inhibitor (secukinumab, ixekizumab), an IL-23 inhibitor (guselkumab, risankizumab), or a JAK inhibitor (tofacitinib, upadacitinib); apremilast as alternative for milder disease
options.B: High-dose systemic corticosteroids long-term as first-line PsA therapy
options.C: NSAIDs alone as monotherapy for moderate disease
options.D: TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor as first-line — avoiding methotrexate as primary axial therapy because MTX has limited efficacy for axial spondyloarthritis; IL-23 inhibitors are also less effective for axial disease per recent comparative trials; appropriate when PsA is AXIAL-PREDOMINANT (sacroiliitis, spondylitis features dominate over peripheral arthritis)

rationale: Psoriatic arthritis with peripheral and dactylitic features is treated per the 2018 ACR/NPF PsA Guideline (Singh JA et al.) and the 2019 EULAR PsA Recommendations (Gossec L et al.). For peripheral PsA (oligoarticular or polyarticular), methotrexate is the conventional DMARD of first choice — it treats both peripheral arthritis and skin psoriasis, and is widely available and inexpensive. For inadequate response or for dactylitis/enthesitis-predominant disease, escalation to a biologic or targeted-synthetic DMARD is indicated, with multiple class options: TNF inhibitor (broad efficacy across PsA domains, also treats axial), IL-17 inhibitor (excellent skin and peripheral efficacy with axial coverage), IL-23 inhibitor (excellent skin and peripheral arthritis but less effective for axial), or JAK inhibitor (oral option). Apremilast is reasonable for milder disease. Long-term high-dose steroids (option B) are avoided because of cumulative toxicity and the risk of psoriasis flare on taper. NSAIDs alone (option C) inadequate for moderate disease with erosions. The axial-predominant regimen (option D) is the appropriate choice when axial features dominate — but this patient has no axial involvement; her phenotype is peripheral + dactylitic.

variants.stem_override: A 38-year-old man with a 6-year history of plaque psoriasis presents to clinic with 8 months of progressive inflammatory back pain (insidious onset, morning stiffness >1 hour, improves with exercise) and bilateral alternating buttock pain. He has minimal peripheral arthritis (occasional knee discomfort) and no dactylitis or significant nail involvement. HLA-B27 positive; ESR 40, CRP 24; RF and anti-CCP negative. MRI SI joints: bilateral active sacroiliitis with bone-marrow edema; lumbar-spine MRI shows scattered Romanus lesions. The clinical picture is AXIAL-PREDOMINANT psoriatic spondyloarthritis.
variants.rationale_for_variant: Mixed perturbation — axial-predominant PsA. Per the 2018 ACR/NPF PsA Guideline and the 2019 EULAR recommendations, the treatment approach for axial-predominant PsA differs from peripheral-predominant disease: (1) METHOTREXATE has LIMITED EFFICACY for axial disease and should not be used as primary axial therapy; (2) TNF inhibitor (preferring monoclonal anti-TNF over etanercept if IBD coexists) and IL-17 inhibitor are the preferred first-line biologic options for axial disease; (3) IL-23 inhibitors are LESS effective for axial PsA than for peripheral/skin per recent comparative-effectiveness evidence and may be deprioritized; (4) NSAIDs are recommended as adjunctive therapy. The correct answer therefore shifts from methotrexate-first (option A) to TNF/IL-17 inhibitor first-line (option D).

variants.stem_override: A 50-year-old man with an 8-year history of plaque psoriasis presents to clinic with new-onset asymmetric oligoarticular arthritis (right wrist, left knee, right second toe with sausage-shaped digit dactylitis), nail pitting and onycholysis, and no axial involvement. RF and anti-CCP negative. ESR 38, CRP 22. Hand X-rays show pencil-in-cup deformity. CASPAR-criteria PsA with peripheral / dactylitic phenotype.
variants.rationale_for_variant: Sex perturbation only — clinical content (peripheral + dactylitic PsA) is unchanged. PsA has roughly equal sex distribution; the management framework with methotrexate first and biologic escalation for dactylitis is sex-independent.
